source_metadata.title: Effects of SGLT2 Inhibitors on Clinical Outcomes, Symptoms, Functional Capacity, and Cardiac Remodeling in Heart Failure: A Comprehensive Systematic Review and Multidomain Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials

source_gaps: README(2).md was not available in the supplied project sources or connected Drive searches.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to integrate randomized heart-failure evidence on SGLT2 inhibitors across clinical outcomes, symptoms and health status, functional capacity, and cardiac structural or metabolic remodeling.
The authors conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review and multidomain meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and prospectively registered the protocol in PROSPERO as CRD420251235850.

Eligible studies were randomized double-blind or open-label trials in adults aged at least 18 years with HFrEF, HFmrEF, or HFpEF, regardless of diabetes status, comparing an SGLT2 inhibitor with placebo or standard care and reporting at least one predefined outcome domain.

population.label: Adults with heart failure
inclusion_criteria: At least one predefined outcome domain
exclusion_criteria: Post hoc secondary reports without extractable data

atoms.canonical_statement: The literature search covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science from inception through 1 February 2025 without language restrictions, with manual screening of references and major heart-failure trial programs.
Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts, resolving disagreements by consensus and, when needed, a third senior reviewer.
Two reviewers independently extracted trial, participant, intervention, and outcome data using a standardized pilot-tested form, with disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer.

Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2 across randomization, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting, with domain-specific judgments when applicable.

The review used random-effects meta-analysis, Hartung-Knapp adjustment in domains with fewer studies, I-squared and Cochran Q for heterogeneity, predefined phenotype and diabetes subgroup analyses, leave-one-out and risk-of-bias sensitivity analyses, and Egger testing when at least 10 studies contributed.
The review reports that 11 randomized trials with 23,812 participants were included, spanning HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF, acute or recently decompensated HF, chronic HF, and a remote digital trial.

population.label: Participants across the included randomized heart-failure trials

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports pooled baseline characteristics of mean age 68.4 years, 34.6% women, 48.2% with type 2 diabetes, mean LVEF 43.8%, and median NT-proBNP 1632 pg/mL.

Nine trials were judged low risk of bias across all domains, while EMPERIAL-Preserved/Reduced and EMPA-VISION raised some concerns because of incomplete allocation-concealment reporting and higher attrition for functional endpoints.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study reports funding from Victor Babes University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Timisoara, Romania.
The authors state that the study used data from previously published articles, created or analyzed no new data, and therefore did not make a new data-sharing resource available.
The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
The principal pooled clinical endpoint was cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalization.

atoms.canonical_statement: The source reports no excess diabetic ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, or volume depletion requiring intervention, and no significant difference in total adverse events, serious adverse events, or treatment discontinuation.

Clinical-outcome heterogeneity was low, KCCQ heterogeneity was moderate, and functional or remodeling heterogeneity was higher; leave-one-out analyses and exclusion of smaller mechanistic trials did not materially change pooled estimates.

source_anchor.paragraph: 3.9 Heterogeneity, Sensitivity Analyses, and Publication Bias

atoms.canonical_statement: For domains with at least 10 contributing estimates, funnel plots were described as symmetric and Egger tests were non-significant with p>0.10.

source_anchor.paragraph: 3.9 Heterogeneity, Sensitivity Analyses, and Publication Bias

atoms.canonical_statement: Trial heterogeneity in symptom and functional endpoints may limit precision of pooled estimates.
KCCQ improvements varied by baseline disease severity and follow-up duration.
Mechanistic and short-duration trials provide complementary but indirect evidence relative to large outcome trials.
Some subgroup analyses, particularly in HFmrEF and HFpEF, were underpowered.
Individual participant data were unavailable, limiting deep phenotyping and participant-level adjustment.
Publication bias cannot be fully excluded despite symmetric funnel plots.
Symptom and functional endpoints were measured over heterogeneous time points ranging from about 6 weeks to 2.6 years.
Small mechanistic trials with sample sizes of about 36 to 84 participants drive the remodeling estimates.
The review did not perform a network meta-analysis against other heart-failure therapies.
Although searches were unrestricted by language, the included full texts were English only.
Most structural imaging data came from HFrEF mechanistic studies, and large HFpEF or HFmrEF trials lacked standardized serial imaging, leaving phenotype-specific remodeling uncertain.
Differences in SGLT2-inhibitor regulatory indications between countries may constrain generalizability across health systems.
Very early KCCQ measurement within 30 days was uncommon, limiting inference about the exact timing of symptom relief.

The authors conclude that SGLT2 inhibitors provide consistent prognostic benefit across the heart-failure spectrum and improve patient-reported health status and functional capacity, while structural and mechanistic findings require more cautious interpretation.
The authors support integrating SGLT2 inhibitors as a key component of guideline-directed heart-failure therapy while calling for additional mechanistic work in HFpEF and acute HF.
